name: The doctrine of The Prince: the ruler's necessary use of deception and force
plain_explanation: A ruler who is always good will be destroyed; he must combine the cunning of the fox with the ferocity of the lion, keeping faith only when it is advantageous, and above all appearing virtuous and religious even when he is not, since most people judge by appearances.
precise_definition: Machiavelli's explicit repudiation of received morality for rulers, illustrated in Chapter XVIII ('In What Way Princes Must Keep Faith'): rulers 'should keep faith when it pays to do so, but not otherwise,' must 'disguise this character well, and... be a great feigner and dissembler,' with Alexander VI cited approvingly as a supreme practitioner of successful deception.
why_it_mattered: This is the doctrine responsible for Machiavelli's notorious reputation ('Machiavellian'), which Russell argues is misunderstood when read in isolation from the Discourses.
historical_origin: Drawn from the political conduct of fifteenth- and early sixteenth-century Italian rulers, especially Caesar Borgia and Pope Alexander VI.
examples: Caesar Borgia's conquest of the Romagna and manipulation of the College of Cardinals
Alexander VI's habitual deception, praised by Machiavelli for its skillful execution
objections: Conventional morality condemns deception and faithlessness as inherently wrong, regardless of political effectiveness
competing_positions: The more republican and liberal doctrine of the Discourses
influence_on_later_thinkers: Gave rise to the term 'Machiavellian' and to a long tradition of realist political theory; Russell explicitly compares it to Hitler's Reichstag fire, 1934 purge, and post-Munich betrayal.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The chapter on ecclesiastical principalities notably conceals Machiavelli's franker views (expressed instead in the Discourses) out of deference to a newly elected Medici pope.
